listings.name: Tempozan Harbor Village
listings.content: Plaza and shopping centre, which houses an aquarium, Ferris wheel, an art gallery, Legoland and a cruise terminal. On the weekend, musicians and street performers offer additional entertainment to people outside the aquarium.

listings.name: Osaka Aquarium Kaiyukan
listings.content: This is one of the world's largest aquariums, with 11,000 tons of water and plenty of sharks (including a whale shark), dolphins, otters, seals, and other sea creatures. The largest tank, representing the Pacific Ocean with 5,400 tons is nothing but overwhelming. Can get intensely crowded, but the aquarium is a spiral featuring the same tanks, and crowds thin out as you get to deeper views of each tank. Back Stage Viewing is available for an additional fee.
listings.price: 2700 adults (16 and over, high school), 1400 child (7-15, elementary school and junior high-school), infant (4-6) 700

listings.name: Tempozan Ferris Wheel
listings.content: One of the largest Ferris wheels, overlooking Osaka Bay and surrounding areas such as Mount Ikoma to the east, Akashi Kaikyō Bridge to the west, Kansai International Airport to the south, and the Rokko Mountains to the north. 17-minute ride. There is an option of a gondola with a see-through floor for no additional cost, but lines for these gondolas tend to be dramatically longer as they are fewer and in greater demand (most report a fairly underwhelming experience too).

listings.name: Naniwa Kuishinbo Yokocho
listings.content: Food theme park (or food court, depending on who you ask), with an aesthetic and theme of nostalgia for the 1960s streets of Osaka. Various Osaka delicacies are available here, including Takoyaki, Okonomiyaki, Kushikatsu, and Ikayaki.

listings.name: Maishima Sludge Center and Maishima Incineration Plant
listings.content: Without a doubt, the best sludge center you've ever seen. The incineration plant makes other waste facilities look like dumps. These two buildings were designed by eccentric Austrian architect Friedensreich Hundertwasser. They are fantastical works that have to be seen to be believed. There are display panels in the lobby of the sludge centre. Tours are available if you contact the facilities in advance, but Hundertwasser's work is on the outside: inside, these are functioning waste treatment facilities. When you arrive, make sure to check the bus schedule to find out when you can leave.

listings.name: Maishima Pottery Village
listings.content: Maishima Pottery Village opened in Osaka’s manmade island in 1998 for the education and promotion of naniwazuyaki, made from the vast amounts of unwanted marine clay which resulted from the construction of Kansai International Airport. The main building has studios with electric and momentum potter’s wheels, rooms for preparing clay and glazes, a gallery, a noborigama climbing kiln and an anagama tunnel kiln. There are also studios for visitors to experience hand-building and painting.
listings.price: 1-day workshop for hand forming ¥500–3500. Additional charge for shipping your work. Booking required.

listings.name: Boat Race Suminoe
listings.content: There's no "bettor" place to see one of Japan's unique gambling sports, hydroplane boat racing, than the race course that typically helps crown the sport's champion every December. If you're interested in placing a bet, you might want to do some research at the official multilingual site of the sport, as there is practically no English guidance available once you arrive.
listings.price: General admission ¥100, reserved seating for additional charge

listings.name: Takopa (Takoyaki Park)
listings.content: Visitors can sample fare from six leading takoyaki shops that Osakans, famously particular about their takoyaki, unreservedly recommend.
listings.price: Admission free, Octopus dumpling ball available for sale at 6 stores

listings.name: Osaka Science Museum
listings.content: Big interactive activity center on several floors. Great for kids. Planetarium and cinema (with science films) downstairs.
listings.price: Adults ¥400, university and high school students ¥300, children free, additional charges for planetarium

listings.name: Osaka Museum of Housing and Living
listings.content: Step back in time as you walk through this life-sized reproduction of an Osaka neighborhood from the 1830s. The street contains re-creations of a public bath (you can borrow a yukata, or cotton kimono, to wear as you stroll around), as well as various shops and merchants' living quarters. There's also a section displaying detailed dioramas of Osaka after the Meiji Period. English-language audio guides are available.
listings.price: Adults ¥600, free for junior-high students, kids, and seniors

listings.name: Umeda Sky Building
listings.content: Built in an attempt to upgrade Osaka's somewhat downbeat Kita district, the project wasn't quite the hoped-for commercial success but this bizarrely shaped 40-story, 173-m building is still a city landmark. Take the escalator through midair to the rooftop observatory for an open-air view of Osaka, which is particularly impressive on a clear night. There is a lover's seat, where if you hold your partner's hand, and each hold a metal button on the seat, the ground around you lights up into a heart. You can purchase an engraved heart lock (¥1000) and attached it to the padlock wall around the seat (padlocks only available after 19:00). Observatory admission ¥2000, 9:30AM-10:30PM daily. The basement features a recreation of a Meiji-era street, with a few small restaurants and bars in appropriate style. There is also a small store downstairs where you can purchase quality mochi on the cheap.
listings.price: Adult ¥2000, children 4-12 ¥500, 50% reduction for those with a disability certificate

listings.name: Japan Mint and Mint Museum
listings.content: It's not widely known even by people from elsewhere in the country that Japan Mint is headquartered in Osaka. For Osakans, Sakura-no-tōrinuke (桜の通り抜け, cherry blossom tunnel road) is a synonym for this facility, attracting a large number of visitors (close to 1 million in just 7 days) during a limited, planned week in mid-Apr. A must-see if you are fond of nature and happen to drop into Osaka in-season. The museum is open 09:00-16:45, is free, and has two floors of coin displays with explanations in Japanese.

listings.name: Osaka Shiki Musical Theater
listings.content: Home of the Shiki Theatre Company, proposing plays and musicals.

listings.name: Zepp Namba
listings.content: A pop club, capacity 2500.

listings.name: Billboard Live Osaka
listings.content: A jazz club, formerly "Blue Note Osaka".
listings.address: Kita Ward, Umeda, 2 Chome−2−22 ハービスPLAZA ENT 地下 2階 B204 nuna 梅田

listings.name: Snack Park
listings.content: Offers okonomiyaki, takoyaki and a few surprises like doteyaki (どて焼き) — stewed beef sinew.

listings.name: Tsuruhashi Fūgetsu
listings.content: Good okonomiyaki as well as yakisoba, with extra toppings (egg, cheese, etc.). The restaurant overlooks Umeda. There's an English menu.

listings.name: Hanadako
listings.content: Standing or to-go takoyaki, very popular with the locals.

listings.name: En (Umeda)
listings.content: En is one of the most atmospheric and tastiest izakayas in Osaka, with branches in Umeda and Namba. The interior is beautiful and food is delicious and reasonably priced. En also has a large range of Japanese sake and has an English menu.
listings.price: Food will cost ¥2000-2500 per person, drinks start from around ¥500

listings.name: Torikizoku
listings.content: Torikizoku is the most popular yakitori chain in Kansai, and can be found near most major stations in Osaka. The food is delicious, comes in generous serves and is very cheap. It's very popular with both locals and expats, and is always busy. Try to come before 7:30PM to secure seats.

listings.name: Endo Sushi
listings.content: Sushi place in Osaka's fish market.

listings.name: Harukoma honten
listings.content: Sushi restaurant located in the Tenjinbashisuji shopping street. Whenever they are open, there is a line outside, mainly composed of locals, so be prepared for a wait of an hour or more.

listings.name: Lupu
listings.content: A gay and lesbian bar owned by a lesbian couple.

listings.name: Cafe de Jumpin' Jumpin'
listings.content: One of Osaka's gay and lesbian bars.

listings.name: Explosion
listings.content: Osaka's most popular and largest (albeit still not very big) gay club. They hold special events on Fridays and Saturdays, some of which are men-only and occasionally women-only, so check their website to make sure that you will be able to enter on the day you plan to visit. Foreigners sometimes get discounts or extra free drink coupons, so bring identification (especially if you are of Asian descent).

listings.name: Jack in the Box
listings.content: A men-only gay nightclub.

listings.name: Sam and Dave
listings.content: Popular international dance club with a meat-market vibe. Two locations in Osaka.

listings.name: J-Hoppers Osaka Central
listings.content: A lively backpackers hostel in the central Osaka. There are three kinds of private rooms (twin, double and triple room). All staff members speak English and can help guests making travel plans. There are also staff who speak French and German. Free WiFi with your laptop or ¥100 per 30 min. for hostel computers. Rental bikes (¥500 per day), with no curfew or lockout and held-luggage services.
listings.price: 8 or 6 bed dorm ¥2500, private rooms ¥3000 per person

listings.name: New Japan Umeda
listings.content: Formerly known as Capsule Inn Osaka. This is Japan's first capsule hotel, designed by noted architect Kisho Kurokawa and opened in 1979. Still open for business, happy to accommodate male foreigners with some semblance of a clue and a steal of a price. No women allowed.
listings.price: ¥2700 for a night, ¥3300 including spa entry

listings.name: Daitoyo
listings.content: Near Umeda, with branches at Namba and Juso. It has a hot spring spa, sauna, and a floor for women.

listings.name: Sunplaza Rinkai
listings.content: Website is in Japanese. The English site can be obtained through an online booking agent if you Google its full name and if vacancies are available an immediate confirmation will be given. Twins beds available. Each apartment has in-suite shower and toilet, A/C, TV, and a kitchenette complete with fridge, stove and cooking utensils.
listings.price: ¥3500 per person per apartment inclusive of taxes, service charges and utilities

listings.name: Hilton Osaka
listings.content: Across the street from JR Osaka station.

listings.name: Hotel Granvia Osaka
listings.content: Next to the JR Osaka Train Station.

listings.name: Imperial Hotel
listings.content: At riverside.

listings.name: Rihga Royal Hotel
listings.content: Opened as the New Osaka Hotel in 1935, this landmark hotel proudly offers one of the best hotel services in town.

listings.name: Ritz-Carlton
listings.content: Japan's first. This particular outlet was voted the best hotel in Japan several times, and has become known as one of the city's swankiest dining and meeting points. Rates start around ¥30,000 a night and rise skyward from there.

listings.name: The Westin Osaka
listings.content: Next to the Umeda Sky Building.

listings.name: Kamigata Ukiyoe Museum
listings.content: (上方浮世絵館) A rather small museum in Nanba dedicated to ukiyoe, Japanese woodblock prints. The interior of the museum looks a bit like an adobe house. It may be most interesting to someone already familiar with the art, as the information inside mostly Japanese only.

listings.name: Sumo Spring Grand Tournament
listings.content: The Osaka Tournament of Japan's national sport, sumo wrestling, is usually held mid-March annually at Osaka Prefectural Gymnasium. Check for schedules and ticket availabilities at the official Nihon Sumo Kyokai homepage.

listings.name: National Bunraku Theater
listings.content: One of the last places in the world where bunraku, a form of intricate puppet theater from the Edo period, can be seen live. The large puppets, which require three operators each, are accompanied by traditional music and narration, and act out great Japanese plays of the 1600s and 1700s. Transcripts in Japanese and synopses in English are provided.

listings.name: ROR Comedy
listings.content: English-language stand-up comedy playhouse.

listings.name: The Silver Ball Planet
listings.content: Pinball arcade featuring over 100 retro, classic & modern pinball machines. ¥100 per play (3 balls) typically, but some are as cheap as ¥10

listings.name: Tamago-yaki stand
listings.content: Best for a snack, this outdoor stall offers a hard-to-find and delicious treat called tamago-yaki, fried egg atop a wide flat sembei cracker with sauce and a variety of toppings available. Much tastier than it sounds.

listings.name: Tsuruhashi Fūgetsu
listings.content: Good okonomiyaki and yakisoba, with extra toppings (egg, cheese, etc.). The restaurant overlooks Umeda. There's an English menu.

listings.name: Tako Tako King
listings.content: This takoyaki place has very friendly staff. Look for the big red octopus wearing a crown.

listings.name: En (Namba)
listings.content: The Namba branch of the excellent En izakaya (see above).
listings.address: 大阪市中央区難波千日前 12-30 難波長和ビル4F

listings.name: Torikizoku
listings.content: Torikizoku is the most popular yakitori chain in Kansai, and can be found near most major stations in Osaka. The food is delicious, comes in generous serves and is very cheap. It's very popular with both locals and expats, and is always busy. Try to come before 19:30 to secure seats.

listings.name: Ajinoya
listings.content: Some of the best okonomiyaki in Osaka, and they're so proud of it they prepare it for you from start to end, making a good choice for the casual visitor as well. The "A set" (¥5,900) includes no less than four styles and will leave four people stuffed to the gills. Very popular, so join the queue early, and beware that ordering here is once and done: you can't add on more later.
listings.address: Namba 1-7-16 現代こいさんビル2F

listings.name: Melbourne Coffee
listings.content: Australian café, serving all day breakfast.
listings.address: 1st Floor Sanei Moor Building, 3-8-7 Minamisenba Chuo-ku

listings.name: Harijyu
listings.content: Shabu-shabu or sukiyaki in Japanese tatami rooms. No reservations are taken except for large groups, so arrive early at nights (18:00 or so) to be sure you get a room without waiting.

listings.name: Kani Dōraku
listings.content: Now a nationwide chain, but this is the original -- although there are three branches around Dotonbori alone! Easily identifiable by the giant mechanical crab waving its pincers about, and as you might guess, the speciality here is crab. The menu runs to pages and pages of ways to prepare the crustaceans, ranging from sushi to hotpots to gratin, but perhaps the most Japanese way is to order o-tsukuri (sashimi) and try your crab legs raw. English menu with easy ordering via tablets.

listings.name: Bar Kama Sutra
listings.content: Small cozy karaoke bar is almost impossible to find but well worth the effort. Foreign and English-speaking Japanese staff, and over 130,000 songs to choose from. The owner, Richard, is a long term resident of Japan and is a wealth of information on what to do and see in the area, where to stay and even where to find work. (No "u" in e-mail address is correct, or: richosaka@gmail.com.)

listings.name: Blarney Stone
listings.content: This pair of Irish pubs have a laid-back atmosphere, friendly staff, and a decent happy hour.

listings.name: Blarney Stone Shinsaibashi
listings.address: Chuo-ku, Higashi Shinsaibashi 2-5-27, Kohda Bldg. B1

listings.name: HUB
listings.content: This British pub chain is at many locations around Osaka, including along Midosuji street in Shinsaibashi, in Namba, and in Chayamachi (Umeda, east side of Hankyu station and walk north a little). HUB serves as a meeting place for many expats as well as Japanese locals. Get there early for happy hour discounts on cocktails (17:00-19:00).

listings.name: G Physique
listings.content: One of Osaka's most popular gay and lesbian bars among foreigners.

listings.name: Club Life
listings.content: Great place to listen to Hip Hop, R&B, Reggae and all black music. Beside playing the latest music, you can also listening the old school classics. Enjoy a wide range of drinks to get you in the party mood or help you relax.
listings.address: Gold Center Building B1F 2-8-12 Higashi Shinsaibashi

listings.name: Clube Joule
listings.content: Packed with trance lovers.

listings.name: Club Pure
listings.content: Extremely crowded dance club. The crowd is around 25-30% international. Be sure to bring your passport, as the ID check here is atypically rigorous. The closest subway station is Namba Station, which is about 5-10 min walk. No dancing is allowed in the club.
listings.price: Cover ¥4000 men, ¥2500 women; includes unlimited drinks but don't lose your cup

listings.name: Guest House U-en
listings.content: The ground floor of this building was once a printing factory, and the upper level was a family home. The guest house has a traditional atmosphere.

listings.name: Asahiplaza Shinsaibashi
listings.content: Sauna available, and there is a separate area for women.

listings.name: B&S Eco-Cube Shinsaibashi
listings.content: Sauna available, and there is a separate area for women.

listings.name: Azu-Garden Nippombashi
listings.content: Online reservation site in English here but you may or may not get a response. If no response, try an online booking agent.
listings.price: Single ¥4,200, double ¥9030, twin ¥9,030 per apartment. All rates inclusive of taxes

listings.name: Kaneyoshi Ryokan
listings.content: This comfortable, modern ryokan is in the heart of downtown on the riverside of Dotombori and very close to the Osaka shopping quarter. English website has an online reservation system.

listings.name: Weekly Green in Namba
listings.content: English website has an online reservation system. It claims to have English-speaking staff on its website so you may attempt an online reservation. If no response, try an online booking agent. Each apartment equipped with in-suite shower and toilet, kitchenette, fridge, portable cooking stove, A/C, TV and telephone.
listings.price: Single ¥4200, twin ¥9450, triple ¥14490, quad ¥18900 per apartment. All rates inclusive of service charge & consumption tax

listings.name: Comfort Inn Shinsaibashi
listings.content: 2 blocks east of Shinsaibashi's central covered shopping arcade, this hotel is a little better than the average business hotel, with clean rooms, English-speaking staff, and a free, generous breakfast buffet.

listings.name: Il Cuore
listings.content: This is a slightly nicer business hotel with larger than average rooms. The hotel provides English language instructions for laundry machines and other hotel services. Breakfast an additional ¥ 1,000.
listings.price: Single ¥9,000 with a double bed for one or two guests

listings.name: Yamatoya Honten
listings.content: A Japanese-style hotel in Dotonbori. There are staff members who can speak English.

listings.name: Best Western Hotel Fino Osaka Shinsaibashi
listings.content: About 5 minutes walking distance from the Shinsaibashi shopping area. Some staff speak good English. The rooms are very small, but very clean.

listings.name: Fraser Residence Nankai
listings.content: Compact but airy and comfortable studio, 1 and 2-bedroom apartments right across the street from Nankai Namba station. Full kitchen and washing facilities make this a great choice for longer stays.

listings.name: Hotel Nikko Osaka
listings.content: Huge Landmark Hotel smack in the middle of Shinsaibashi along tree lined Mido-suji Avenue. Rooms are comfortable and have amazing views at night as hotel is the tallest building in the immediate area. Attached to Shinsaibashi train station and close to Amerika-mura, shopping, and night-life.

listings.name: Hotel New Otani Osaka
listings.content: A luxury business hotel in Osaka, Japan offering accommodation, 13 restaurants and bars, vacation packages and meeting rooms. This five-star hotel is in the Osaka Business Park near Osaka Castle.

listings.name: Swissôtel Nankai
listings.content: Next to Namba train and bus stations.

listings.name: Open Air Museum of Old Farmhouses
listings.content: Ryokuchi park is lovely, and in it is a museum of a dozen old Edo period farmhouses, moved across country and lovingly reconstructed. Also on display are tools, furniture, and the like. You can go to Himeji-jo or the old palace in Kyoto and see how the rulers lived, but come down here to see how the people lived. Thanks to the efforts of a volunteer from Australia, they have a great new English-language brochure to guide you.

listings.name: Osaka municipal indoor pool - Yodogawa
listings.content: Heated swimming pool & exercise room.

listings.name: Shin-Osaka Youth Hostel
listings.content: A clean, modern, and friendly youth hostel.

listings.name: Mystays Shin Osaka
listings.content: Small, clean rooms and a bit of a hike to the bullet train station, but unbeatable for the price. Some staff speak English. Some rates include buffet breakfast in the hotel's restaurant (¥1100 separately). Family Mart and Lawson convenience stores are a half-block away, while there is a 7-Eleven with international ATM access is on the way from Shin-Osaka station.
listings.price: Web site lists singles starting from ¥8300, though cheaper rates might be found when searching for availability

listings.name: Osaka Castle
listings.content: Osaka's best known sight, although it's a concrete reconstruction that pales in comparison with, say, Himeji. Think of it as a museum built in the shape of a castle, rather than as an historical Japanese castle, as the interior consists of several gloomy modern galleries rather than a real reconstruction. Still, it's pretty enough from the outside, especially in the cherry blossom season when Osakans flock to the castle park to picnic and make merry. Naniwa Palace Site Park or Naniwanomiya can also be found south to Osaka Castle Park (although it's one of Japan's oldest habitats and palace sites, today it's little more than an empty grass field where the outlines of Naniwa's palace foundations from around 643 AD have been partly recreated in concrete).
listings.price: Adults ¥1200, university/high school students ¥600, children 15 and below free

listings.name: Osaka Museum of History
listings.content: An ideal place to learn all-abouts of Osaka's history. Enjoyable view over Osaka Castle and the OBP skyscrapers.

listings.name: Peace Osaka
listings.content: A museum dedicated to the promotion of peace through displays of war. Because it is an Osaka museum, it largely focuses on the effects of the bombings on Osaka in World War II. In the past, the museum also had exhibitions depicting the atrocities committed by Japan against China, Korea, and Southeast Asia. Sadly, however, those exhibitions were permanently removed in 2015 in response to pressure from conservative political groups. Exhibits have English explanations.

listings.name: National Bunraku Theater
listings.content: One of the last places in the world where bunraku, a form of intricate puppet theater from the Edo period, can be seen live. The large puppets, which require three operators each, are accompanied by traditional music and narration, and act out great Japanese plays of the 1600s and 1700s. Transcripts in Japanese and synopses in English are provided.

listings.name: Jo-Terrace
listings.content: A cluster of midrange restaurants and cafes in an attractive wooden complex inspired by a traditional jōkamachi, the shopping district below a castle. A good place for a post-castle coffee or meal.

listings.name: CarpeDiem Inn
listings.content: Traditional-style house and garden within walking distance of the Shiroyama Temple.

listings.name: Super Hotel Osaka Tanimachi 4-Chome
listings.content: Mid-price chain hotel, around a corner from the Tanimachi 4-chome subway station and a 7-Eleven store with ATM that accepts foreign cards. Modern and clean but compact rooms, with a free Japanese breakfast and free WiFi included with all stays.

listings.name: Sumiyoshi Grand Shrine
listings.content: One of Japan's oldest Shinto shrines, with a history stretching back 1800 years. Its traditional architecture is unusual among Japan's shrines, and its park-like surroundings with the sacred bridge arching over a tranquil pond make it a restful break from the busy environment of Osaka.

listings.name: Tobita Shinchi
listings.content: This is Japan's largest red-light district outside Tokyo, where ladies pose at genkan entrances Amsterdam-style to attract clientele, accompanied by an older woman (called a yarite-baba or mama-san) who serves as the pimp and collects money from customers. However, this place is arguably more interesting to walk through than its Amsterdam counterpart, and most of the brothels operate out historic buildings dating back to the Taisho era (1912-1926), giving visitors a rare glimpse into what Japanese red-light districts looked like before the prostitution ban came into effect in 1958. No photographs allowed, even in the streets! Women walking through the area will be met with stern looks from the mama-san making it clear that they are not welcome, and even foreign men have long been unwelcome, though that is gradually changing as a few of the brothels have started accepting foreign customers if they can speak Japanese. If you don't mind that, it is well worth the experience, even if you just came for the looks.

listings.name: Cerezo Osaka
listings.content: The local J. League soccer team plays at Nagai Stadium.

listings.name: Nagai Stadium
listings.content: Nagai Stadium is the home of the professional soccer team Cerezo Osaka.

listings.name: Taiyoshi Hyakuban
listings.content: Most of the "restaurants" in the area are really brothels in disguise (since prostitution is illegal in Japan), but this extravagant century-old brothel is a Tangible Cultural Property that has been turned into an actual restaurant open to the public. Specialities include hot pot dishes like sukiyaki and yosenabe.

listings.name: Hiro's Guesthouse
listings.content: Hiro's Guesthouse is in the heart of Koreatown in Osaka. It is a little far from the station, but in a nice, social neighbourhood. The open first floor of the guesthouse is very social and great to hang out and make friends at. Hiro and the others go out of their way to help and ensure you have a good time - this is more than just a place to sleep at.
listings.price: Dormitory ¥2500, private rooms ¥3500 per person, free Wifi and computer use

listings.name: Osaka Municipal Nagai Youth Hostel
listings.price: ¥3000 per person per night, ¥1000 dinner, ¥500 breakfast

listings.name: Nagai Park Hotel
listings.price: Single room: ¥6500 per person per night including breakfast. Twin room: ¥6500 per person per night including breakfast

listings.name: Tsūtenkaku
listings.content: While the original tower was built early 20th century, the current "newer" version is designed by the same Prof. Naitō, who also designed Tokyo Tower. This landmark built in the middle of the Shinsekai (新世界) area is a symbol of reconstruction of the City of Osaka post World War II. There's a "Sky Billiken" on the platform, definitely makes your wishes come true, once you rub his feet! And if you are lucky, your guide will have another job as a comedian!
listings.price: Trip to the top ¥600, outside platform with guide and safety belt extra ¥1400

listings.name: Shitennōji Temple
listings.content: The temple was built by Emperor Suiko in 593 AD. Although the current buildings are mostly post World War II reconstructions, the temple is a rare sample which conveys the continental style (notably the positioning of the individual buildings inside the complex) of 6th-7th century to present.

listings.name: Abeno Harukas Tower
listings.content: Being Osaka's tallest building, this tower features malls, restaurants, shops and offices. Most interesting for tourists is probably the Abeno Harukas Art Museum (changing exhibitions, around ¥1300) and the observation deck Harukas 300 on 60th floor in 300 m height (¥1350). If you want to get a good view of the city for free, take elevators and escalators to 17F, then change into one of the business elevators to 30F. There are large glass windows on all sides of the building offering views onto all of Osaka for free!

listings.name: Tennoji Zoo
listings.content: The zoo has animals from African Savanna, Asian tropical rainforest, aviary, polar bears, penguins and sea lions.

listings.name: Osaka City Museum of Fine Arts
listings.content: The museum focuses on Japanese and east Asian art.
listings.price: Adults ¥300, high school and university students ¥200, elementary school students and under free

listings.name: Spa World
listings.content: Gender-separated European and Asian-themed spas and saunas as well as a pool for the family with slides and fun (don't forget your swimming trunks). Open 24 hr so it is handy if you're stuck for accommodation or locked out of your hotel after a night on the town, just pay up, change into their cotton overalls and pass out on one of their comfy leather recliners with as many blankets as you like. Try the outdoor onsen (try not to get burnt in the sun) or watch their huge TV in their bar with a cold beer. The gym also available to you as part of the entry fee, but other facilities like massages and body scrubs, cost extra. "Rollover" for day passes is at 09:00 on the dot. Well worth spending an afternoon chilling out here. People with tattoos, permanent or temporary, are barred from using the facilities.
listings.price: ¥1500 for all day (¥500 extra if using the pool); extra charge ¥1450 for entering, staying, or leaving between 00:00-05:00

listings.name: Osaka Municipal Tennoji Sports Center
listings.content: Heated swimming pool & exercise room.

listings.name: Jan-Jan Yokocho Street
listings.content: Jan-Jan Yokocho is a famous shopping street along a narrow lane. There are still many establishments running in the same shops they built immediately after World War II. The entire area is squashed with small, cheap eating houses.

listings.name: Kushikatsu Daruma Shinsekai Main Shop
listings.content: The original Shinsekai shop of Osaka's most famous kushikatsu institution, with its trademark grumpy uncle statue admonishing diners not to double-dip their skewers into the shared sauce pots. Order a 13-piece Shinsekai set for an easy sampler of this Osakan classic and wash it down with draft beer or a whiskey highball. If there's a queue at the original outlet (and there usually is), there are two other Darumas right around the corner with the same food, more spacious seating, and less lines.

listings.name: Hotel Pivot
listings.content: Western and Japanese style rooms available. Rooms are simple, but clean. Traditional Japanese bath with communal showers and hot pool open to men and women during separate opening times in the morning and evening. Three additional private showers are available 24 hr. Showers and bath are on the ground floor. Wireless internet in rooms plus three internet connected computers in the lobby. Free tea and coffee in the mornings. No communal kitchen, but microwave and boiling water available in lobby. No curfew.

listings.name: Hotel Mikado
listings.content: Free use internet and kitchen.

listings.name: Hotel Toyo
listings.content: Some Japanese people seem to use this place as a de facto apartment, which is a testament to the low price and convenience of the hotel. Each room contains a futon, a fan/heater or AC, and TV. There is a shower room on the first floor, or you can use the public bath of the neighboring Hotel Taiyo for free. Internet is available in the small lounge for free, and free WiFi is available on every floor.
listings.price: Single without AC ¥1500, with AC ¥1700; ¥1000 discount for reservation 10 days in advance or more

listings.name: Hotel Taiyo
listings.content: Free internet available in the lobby and nice rooms with a clean futon, TV, & fridge. Friendly staff at reception with minimal English and beer vending machine. Communal toilets and washroom with bath, sometimes can see Yakuza members in the washroom with their irizumi (tattoos)!

listings.name: Hotel TRW
listings.content: No Wifi.

listings.name: OMO7 Osaka
listings.content: Located right next to Shinsekai, this large, arty hotel by the Hoshino Resort group is the first upscale hotel in the area and has been variously hailed and condemned as an example of gentrification. The starkly modernist bathhouse on the 2nd floor is also open to the public (¥1000).

listings.name: Hirano Old City
listings.content: A rare surviving example of a medieval moated city that was rebuilt in the early Edo period with a grid-patterned layout. While most of the moats were filled in during modern urban development, the district preserves its historical atmosphere through its orderly grid of streets lined with traditional Edo-period machiya and numerous historic temples and shrines.

listings.name: Kire Moated Settlement
listings.content: Explore Osaka City's best-preserved moated settlement. This townscape retains the traditional form of a moated settlement dating back to the Middle Ages.

listings.name: Hirano "Machigurumi" Museum
listings.content: Town-wide ecomuseum network started in 1993; the walk between the 16 museums is part of the experience. Internationally recognized as one of Japan's pioneering ecomuseum initiatives, it is organized entirely by local residents, with no government involvement.

listings.name: Katana Museum
listings.content: Small sword museum attached to Masumian, with displays and sword polishing demonstrations.

listings.name: Cotton City Museum
listings.content: Museum in the kura of the registered Ebisui House, showing tools used in yarn production.

listings.name: Kumata Shrine
listings.content: Established in 861 (Jogan 3), this ancient Shinto shrine serves as the guardian of the Hirano Old City. It is also famous for its dynamic summer festival called Hirano-gō Summer Festival held annually in July, featuring traditional Danjiri float processions.

listings.name: Hirano-gō Summer Festival
listings.content: The largest danjiri festival in Osaka, and among summer festivals it ranks second only to the Tenjin Festival in scale. Rooted in the Heian-period “Gion-e” tradition, which shares its origins with Kyoto’s Gion Festival, it attracts as many as 300,000 visitors from across Osaka to experience the raw energy of the danjiri floats and the sacred dignity of the mikoshi procession. Held July 11–14.

listings.name: Senkō-ji Temple
listings.content: A temple of the Koyasan Shingon sect, traditionally said to have been founded by Prince Shotoku in the early 7th century. It is widely renowned for its interactive "Jigoku-do" (Hell Hall), which provides a vivid, visual depiction of Buddhist purgatory and judgment to teach the consequences of bad actions. The temple grounds also feature a small museum dedicated to retro snacks and toys from the Showa era.
listings.price: Free for the main temple grounds (¥100 entry fee for the Hell Hall)

listings.name: Dainenbutsu-ji Temple
listings.content: The head templesōhonzan of the Yūzū-Nembutsu sect (融通念佛宗). Its massive wooden main hall (hondō) is the largest wooden building in Osaka Prefecture and a registered tangible cultural property.It is famous for the spectacular Manbu Onenri (万部おねり) festival (early May 1–5), featuring a grand procession of 25 bodhisattvas, music, and dance — designated an Osaka City Intangible Folk Cultural Property.

listings.name: Ganko Hirano-gō Yashiki
listings.content: Japanese restaurant in a 400-year-old merchant house, with a garden and a small living-culture museum attached.
